blocks.prompt: The Hamster With Pockets in Its Cheeks
blocks.text: A hamster has a pocket in each cheek. The pockets are made of stretchy skin. They reach all the way back to its shoulders. When a hamster finds seeds, it does not eat them right away. It stuffs them into its cheeks. Its head grows fat and wide. Then it runs down into its burrow under the ground. It pushes the seeds out with its paws and stacks them in a little room. That room is its pantry. A hamster sleeps all day and works all night.

blocks.prompt: The Animal Named After Hoarding
blocks.text: The word hamster comes from a German word, hamstern, which means to hoard. It is a good name. A hamster spends its nights gathering food and carrying it home, and it almost never eats where it finds a meal. Its cheek pouches are two bags of loose skin that stretch from its mouth back to its shoulders. A hungry hamster can pack them until its head looks twice as wide. Then it hurries down into its burrow and pushes the load out with its front paws. A wild hamster's burrow is not one hole. It is a set of rooms joined by tunnels, dug a few feet down. There is a nest room lined with soft grass, a bathroom room, and a pantry stacked with seeds. The pantry matters. Winter is long, food is scarce, and a hamster that hoards well is a hamster that lives until spring. Hamsters sleep through the day and wake at dusk. In the wild they travel a long way each night to fill those cheeks.

blocks.prompt: One Burrow, Nearly Every Hamster
blocks.text: In 1930, a zoologist named Israel Aharoni went looking for an animal that most scientists thought was already gone. The golden hamster had been described once, back in 1839, from a single specimen. After that, for ninety years, nobody found another one. Near the city of Aleppo, in Syria, Aharoni's team dug into a wheat field and opened a burrow several feet down. Inside was a mother golden hamster and her litter of pups. He carried them back to Jerusalem in a box. Most of that litter did not survive the trip and the weeks that followed. Some chewed straight through their wooden cage and vanished into the walls. Only a handful were left to breed. That handful is the reason you can meet a hamster in a pet store today. Nearly every golden hamster on Earth, in homes and in laboratories, descends from those few survivors. Their young were shipped from Jerusalem to England, then on to the United States, and the numbers grew quickly, because a golden hamster is pregnant for only about sixteen days. That is one of the shortest pregnancies of any mammal. Meanwhile, back in Syria, the wild golden hamster has not done well. Its home is farmland, and farmland keeps changing. Scientists now list the species as vulnerable, which means it is at real risk of disappearing. Think about how odd that is. As a pet, this animal is everywhere. As a wild animal, it is barely holding on in the fields where it belongs.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.
The Animal That Is Mostly Pantry
blocks.text: A hamster is built around one idea: take it home, and take it home now. Start with the pouches. A hamster's cheeks are not cheeks the way yours are. They are two loose bags of skin running from the corners of the mouth back along the head to the shoulders, and they contain no spit glands, so the cargo stays dry. A feeding hamster works fast, sorting seeds with its paws and packing them in until its skull seems to double in width. Then it leaves. The eating happens later, underground, where nothing is watching. The burrow it returns to is a small piece of engineering. Tunnels drop a few feet into the soil and open into rooms with jobs: a nest of shredded grass, a bathroom kept well away from the food, and one or more chambers used as a pantry. Wild hamsters are not casual about the pantry. People digging out the burrows of the wild European hamster have found pounds of grain stacked underground, sorted, clean, and dry. This explains the shape of the whole animal. A hamster is small, edible, and alone. It has no herd, no lookouts posted on a rock, and famously poor eyesight. What it has is speed, a hole in the ground, and a pantry it filled in the dark while the owls were busy somewhere else. The hoarding is not greed. It is the entire plan. Now the strange part. Put a hamster in a cage with a wheel and food it never has to search for, and it will still run. Not a little. A hamster can cover several miles in one night on a wheel, going nowhere at all. Researchers once set running wheels outdoors in a quiet field and filmed what happened. Wild mice found them, climbed on, and ran, with no food offered and no reward of any kind. Whatever a hamster is doing on that wheel, it did not learn from the cage. It arrived with it.

blocks.prompt: The Hamster That Ate Only Corn
blocks.text: For most of recorded history, the European hamster was a problem. It is a far bigger animal than the pet you know, roughly the size of a loaf of bread, with a black belly and white patches, and it lived across the grain fields of Europe from France to Russia. It dug, it hoarded, and what it hoarded was the harvest. Farmers dug out its burrows and took the grain back. Governments paid bounties for its skin, and in some years hundreds of thousands were killed. In 2020, the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved the European hamster onto its list of critically endangered species, warning that it could vanish within about thirty years. In under a century, an animal hunted as a pest had become an animal running out of time. Nobody set out to do that. The interesting question is how it happened anyway. Part of the answer is ordinary. The fields changed. Hedgerows came out, plowing went deeper, harvests arrived earlier and left less behind, and a hamster that wakes from hibernation into a bare, chemically clean field is a hamster with nothing to hoard. Part of the answer is stranger, and it came out of a French laboratory. Researchers had noticed that hamster mothers in corn-growing regions were doing something appalling: giving birth normally, then eating their own pups within days. So they tested the diet directly. One group of hamsters was fed wheat, another corn, each with clover or worms alongside. The wheat-fed mothers raised about four out of five of their pups. The corn-fed mothers raised almost none. Those animals ran in circles, their tongues turned dark, and their blood ran thick and wrong. The cause turned out to be a vitamin. Corn is poor in niacin, and the niacin it does contain is chemically bound up in a form animals cannot absorb. Humans learned this the hard way. Whole regions that lived mainly on corn suffered pellagra, a niacin-deficiency disease of rashes, confusion, and death, and the cause was not pinned down until the 1930s. The peoples of Mexico and Central America had solved it thousands of years earlier by soaking corn in lime water, a process called nixtamalization, which unlocks the vitamin. The hamsters of the French farmland had no such option. When a field is corn from one horizon to the other, a hoarder's greatest strength inverts into a trap. It fills its pantry perfectly, and its pantry starves it. That is the part worth sitting with. The hamster did nothing wrong. It performed the behavior that had carried its species for thousands of years, exactly as well as it always had. We changed what grew in the field, and the behavior kept running anyway. There are people working on it now. Programs in France and Germany breed hamsters and release them, and pay farmers to plant strips of wheat, alfalfa, and clover between the rows of corn. In a few places the numbers have ticked upward. It is a small repair, and a slow one, and it tells you the true shape of the problem. Saving this animal turns out not to be about the animal at all. It is about what we plant.
